latin.623: sed immediatam & antecedentem, quam Vir doctus communem appellat & ita describit Cap. 1. §. xiii. Imputatio, inquit, peccati Adami communis est, qua peccatum Adami non ipsum modo reum fecit, sed etiam totum genus, quod in ipso seminaliter & radicaliter continebatur, eodem reatu implicuit, iam ab eo tempore, quo lapsus est Adam.
latin.624: Et paulo post inquit: Existente autem humana natura in individuo illo principiali, in illo etiam dici possunt homines communiter extitisse. Extiteruntne scilicet a persona Adami distantes & separati? Non arbitror quenquam hoc dicturum. Et Cap. 2. §. xvii. Communis, inquit, illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adami transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cuiuscumque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia atque adeo etiam corruptione illa quae in singulos naturali generatione descendit, quatenus ab initio resuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo.
latin.625: Facta est igitur ista imputatio cum nondum essemus personae separatae & distantes ab Adamo: vel, ut loquitur is quicum mihi res erat, cum consideraremus a Deo tanquam unus homo in Adamo. Nunc, opinor, quam vim habeat argumentum, ipse per te, Lector, satis intelligis.
latin.626: Rectius igitur mea sententia fecisses, si Calvini interpretationi acquiescens non contempsisses id quod legere potuisti in Clavi Scripturae ad nomen peccatum, his verbis: significat quoque crebro verbum חטא peccavit in prima conjugatione non actionem, sed qualitatem inhaerentem, seu sortem ac conditionem hominis, seu esse peccatorem, esse reum, sicut solent verba hebraea saepissime tantum existentiam rei, non actionem aut passionem aliumve motum indicare.
latin.627: Et paulo post: sic Rom. v. in Adamo omnes peccaverunt: id est, scelerati ac Dei hostes fuerunt. Quae quasi habitualis significatio verbi & nominis peccati diligenter observanda est.
latin.628: Et rursus, Romanorum quinto: sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo omnes peccaverunt: non actionem sed potius habituale, aut sortem innatum & essentiale malum significat, quod nempe per Adamum omnes facti sint corrupti &c.

pass_a.623: Placeus now names his target after sparing mediate imputation: the immediate and antecedent kind Garrigues calls 'common.' On Cap. 1 §13, Adam's sin made not only Adam guilty but implicated the whole race contained in him seminaliter in the same reatus from the moment of the fall.
pass_a.624: He presses Garrigues's Cap. 2 §17 wording: that common/immediate imputation is later than Adam's first actual transgression yet prior to each descendant's personal existence and the corruption that descends by generation—because from the beginning all were commonly in Adam, not already as separate persons distant from him.
pass_a.625: Therefore the imputation was made when we were not yet separate persons from Adam—or, in the interlocutor's phrase, when God considered us as one man in Adam. Placeus thinks the reader can now see for himself what force his earlier omnes argument has.
pass_a.626: Better, he says, to rest with Calvin and not slight the Clavis Scripturae on peccatum: Hebrew 'sinned' (Qal) often means an inherent quality or condition—being a sinner, being guilty—not a discrete action, just as Hebrew verbs often mark a thing's existence rather than motion.
pass_a.627: Calvin's follow-on gloss for Rom 5: 'all sinned in Adam' means they were wicked and enemies of God. Placeus insists that quasi-habitual sense of the verb and noun 'sin' be carefully kept in view.
pass_a.628: Tip from the same Clavis on Rom 5:12: 'in whom all sinned' signifies not an action but an innate and essential evil lot—namely that through Adam all have been made corrupt. Tip before the aptitudo examples, Sohnius, and Zanchius on peccare actu.

623: But the immediate and antecedent imputation, which the learned man calls "common" and so describes in Cap. 1 §13: "The common imputation of Adam's sin," he says, "is that by which Adam's sin made not only him guilty, but also implicated the whole race, which was contained in him seminaliter and radicaliter, in the same guilt, already from the time when Adam fell."
624: And a little later he says: "But with human nature existing in that principal individual, men can also be said to have existed commonly in him." Existed, that is, distant and separate from Adam's person? I do not think anyone will say that. And Cap. 2 §17: "That common or immediate [imputation]," he says, "just as it was later than Adam's first actual transgression, so it was prior to the personal existence of each man born of Adam, and so also to that corruption which descends into individuals by natural generation, insofar as from the beginning all flowed commonly in Adam."
625: That imputation was therefore made when we were not yet persons separate and distant from Adam—or, as the one I was dealing with puts it, when we were considered by God as one man in Adam. Now, I think, you yourself, reader, sufficiently see what force the argument has.
626: You would therefore, in my judgment, have done better if, resting in Calvin's interpretation, you had not despised what you could read in the Clavis Scripturae under the name peccatum. He writes that the verb "sinned" in the Qal conjugation often signifies not an action, but an inherent quality, or a man's lot and condition, or to be a sinner, to be guilty—just as Hebrew verbs very often indicate only the existence of a thing, not an action or passion or other motion.
627: And a little later: so Rom. 5, in Adam all sinned—that is, they were wicked and enemies of God. Which quasi-habitual sense of the verb and noun "sin" is to be carefully observed.
628: And again, Romans 5: as through one man sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men, in whom all sinned. It signifies not an action but rather a habitual, or innate and essential, evil lot: namely that through Adam all have been made corrupt, etc.
